utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Just as a preliminary housekeeping matter, I would just note that there is one exhibit under seal for which there was no need for if to be under seal and that ask Exhibit 163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that can be unsealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 163, very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, forgive me for rising. There are special measures in place for this witness and I can see his image on the screen in the public gallery. I also note there is no microphone there for voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I should say in comfort for the witness his image is now off the screen and was only there momentarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm looking at another screen showing it in a distorted form. I see the electronic box behind you, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I see the one the public sees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm not sure we have some other technical difficulty we're addressing. Perhaps I'll just wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think if you commence, Mr. Shin, we'll see whether it's in order now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, when we broke off on Friday, you were telling us about a meeting in Klecka with Celiku and others. Was Qerqiz present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the beginning of the sentence. Could he -- ask him to repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sorry, the translators didn't hear the beginning of the sentence. Could you please repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know I said. It is possible that he was there where the meeting took place in that room earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you say that, I'm referring now to the meeting in the room where Celiku and as you say approximately 10 other persons were there. Just to be clear, do you know whether Qerqiz was in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I'm trying to explain. I said I'm not sure whether he entered that particular room or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: On Friday you also told us a few names of people who were there and units that were represented there. You mentioned a Kumanova, Gazetari and the leader of the Guri unit. I'd like to ask you first, did you at that time know the full name of the person known as Gazetari?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you learn the true name of that person later on?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what did you learn it to be?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Shukri Buja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How did you learn that that was his name?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that through the media, through television. I don't know for sure. I saw that it appeared several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when it was that you learned his true name?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Apart from the persons that you have named previously and whom I listed just now, were there any other persons whose name or the name of whose unit you recall being present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Apart from what I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, have you ever heard of a unit called the Pellumbi unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was anyone from that unit present at that meeting in Klecka with Celiku and others?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also someone whose name I don't remember whom I knew before. I talked with him. I'm not certain whether he was from Pellumbi unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How long was this meeting as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't last long. I can't tell you for certain. I knew -- I know that it was interrupted because of some shelling nearby, and I think that was the reason for the interruption of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You had testified on Friday that your unit, you joined that unit in Malisevo and came with them from Rrasat e Rrahovecit to assist Celiku. These other persons at this meeting, and the other units that were represented, do you know where they were based?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which unit are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's begin with the Guri unit. You had testified that someone from the Guri unit was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And my question is: Did you know whether the Guri unit was normally based, if you know.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you know where Gazetari was normally based?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him there at the headquarters, and I thought he belonged there. Also, about the units that reported there, the people who represented those units whom I didn't know their names, whose names I didn't know, I thought that they too belonged to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you explain, if possible, why it was that you believed that they belonged to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed so because I was there where everyone was reporting, and this is where I thought that they were -- belonged to the staff, to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, how long did you stay at Klecka on that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, when the meeting was interrupted because of the shelling nearby, that was why we left the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you go from Klecka to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Divjake village. From there I went to Novoselle, to the unit where I belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Novoselle, with that unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure. Maybe it was on the next day that I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Where did you go when you left?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to towards some villages with a small lorry. There were two people who accompanied us. I don't know exactly where the places we went through. I know that we used the asphalt road, the road from Orahovac to Malisevo. There is a village, Marali, it's called there. And I know that it was early morning when we arrived in Panorc village where we stayed until the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And why was it -- why was it that you left Novo Selo at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that through the radio communication we received a message from Jablanice, that is, that it was attacked. And I think that the news arrived at Klecka at the headquarters from where we received orders to go to Jablanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you speak to anyone before leaving from Novo Selo?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with a soldier who escorted us on the way whose name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who made the decision -- who made the decision to leave Novo Selo?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the news that came from Jablanice, the entire unit agreed to leave. But as to the decision, I don't know who made the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if you can remember who -- who told -- how did you learn, how did you learn about the message from Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that I knew that we had some radio contacts. As far as I remember, the soldier who came with us, who came to call us, who brought the lorry, we was with another person and he told us that we had to go there. But I don't remember exactly whether we talked about the person who had given the order. This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the soldier who came with you, do you know what unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. It is the same person who came and called me to go to Klecke. It's the same person who came with us. I can't remember his name. I never learned his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would object at this juncture on the grounds of hearsay, an observation that I normally do not raise, because the questions asked and the responses given do not even meet a threshold of reliability with regard to the information received. There's no identification whatsoever of any speakers other than a soldier who is unidentified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. A person unidentified; I know that you can say that is no identification, but in the practice here it can be. So that we are well aware that it may be that little can be attached to that, but it doesn't technically rule itself out on that footing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate the Court's ruling, and I am more concerned just to highlight the point than to -- to believe that based on the evidence thus adduced that I would obtain the kind of relief that I would in other jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have to live in the jurisdiction where we are, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, on Friday, you had testified that the Lapusnik gorge was overtaken by the Serbs. My final question on this -- in this area to you is: Do you know what -- do you know when that meeting in Klecka with Celiku and others, when that occurred in relation to the overtaking of Lapusnik gorge by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was a few days after that. I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could please go into private session for the next area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. 23 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, you testified on Friday that you had registered with the KLA at -- at the barracks, a barracks were soldiers were staying. How many soldiers were staying there, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 10 or 15 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And did you -- did you yourself stay at that barracks at some point?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you mean Jablanice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do mean Jablanica. Approximately how long did you stay there at those barracks?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how long we stayed, but even after I left that place, I used to go there quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You -- do you know approximately when it was that you stayed there, even if I don't recall exactly how long it was that you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the time I went there or...

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question wasn't clear. Can you tell us what -- when it was that you were staying at the barracks in Jablanica, and you can do that by what month or months it is was, or by any other way that you can explain that.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there when I first went. That is, in April. Up to early May. But during the time we also left the place, we went to other places, to other surrounding villages. After 21st of May, I remember that I personally went back there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could just focus on -- on April first -- sorry, on the month of April. Apart from the 10 or 15 soldiers including yourself staying there, was there -- did you see anybody else who was there?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen, but I'm not getting the point of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any persons who were being detained there?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When did you first become aware of this?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that for the first time on the day I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you see anyone who was being detained there at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afrim Morina, from Gjakova, someone by the name of Idriz, he was from Polac of Drenica. He lived in Prizren at that time before he was taken to that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you describe to us where in those barracks you saw those two people?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the same building where I too stayed for some days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us more specifically where in that building you saw these two people?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same building that I stayed, meaning that this was the only building that was like a barracks, if you like, where soldiers stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could ask it this way: Could you please describe the barracks, the physical layout?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is located at the -- the exit of Jablanice village. In the direction where you live Jablanica, in the direction of Decane. It is on the right side of the road. There were two big wooden gates. One part of it was covered. When you enter the gate on the left side of the yard, there is a small house with four rooms. It is a bit higher from the ground. It had a small cellar when you entered it, on the left side, in the next room -- in the second room was where we stayed. That was the place where I saw those two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the room where you saw those two persons, was -- was the door locked?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were there -- were there any guards at the door?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that there were guards in the proper sense of the word because we soldiers could go in, could go out. There wasn't somebody designated to be a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were there any guards at the house, if not actually at the door?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the entrance we used to -- to be guard, to stand there and guard in shifts by three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, turning back to the two persons that you say that you saw there and beginning with Afrim Morina. What was his physical condition when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to know Afrim Morina, but when I saw him there, he wasn't in a good state. He was beaten. There were some signs on his face. He used to wear glasses, reading glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The translation said that there were some signs on his face. Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Signs, meaning when somebody hits you, you know, and you can find the injuries, you can see the marks of injuries or the scars on the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what was the physical condition, as far as you saw, of the other person, this Idriz?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: His physical condition was also bad. He was shrunk. He too had signs or marks. I can't tell you whether there were many of them or not, but there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Why were these two persons being held there?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, from what I heard there, also from Afrim directly and also from Idriz, Idriz came from Drenica, and he said that he had talked with someone from the KLA there. He came to Dukagjin plateau to find someone to find arms. Afrim was his friend. Afrim was someone who had been engaged in activities or in the organisation field regarding the Kosovo issue. They met and they came together. And they asked for weapons. I'm not clear but this is how it was then. This is what both of them told me. When they came to the headquarters, they were told that, We will talk with the leader who sent you here. Idriz said to me that somebody which the pseudonym of Lisi, this is what he told me, that is Idriz, after contacting that certain Lisi, they told him that you are lying, nobody has sent you. You have come here to gather information and this is where the bad thing that happened to them started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you say that this is when the bad thing that happened to them started, could you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this I mean their maltreatment. And the scars and the signs that I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know how long those two were in that barracks in detention in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I know that when I went there, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you say roughly. Were they there for more than a week or less than a week?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't discuss this so I cannot tell you whether it was one or two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know what ultimately happened to Afrim Morina and to this Idriz?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Afrim much later, maybe it was even earlier that I met him, but I remember meeting him sometime in August. I'm not certain about the time. I can describe the conversation I had with him. He told me that I left and I went to Baran, in Azem municipality [phoen] [as interpreted], under the command of Tahir Zema. They had barracks there. It was in August after I returned to Jablanica for some days. I was in Jablanica with some friends of mine whom I knew from the past, when I was a soldier, and I said so him, Are you coming? No, he said, because you know what I have been through. I know that he told me that he was injured at the entrance to Gllogjan. I said I went there as reinforcements and he was injured on his arm. He showed me the wound. He showed me also about Idriz. He said, Yes they accepted him as a soldier. He participated in the attack on Jablanica. He wasn't good enough and he was killed by the Serbs. Then he was massacred, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, when you say that Afrim told you that hes with a soldier and that Idriz had become a soldier, what -- who were they soldiers for? Was that -- I'll leave it at that: Who were they soldiers for?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were KLA soldiers, but I -- but I know that Afrim went to Jaran [phoen], whereas Idriz to Jablanice headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you see other people who were being detained at those barracks in the month of April?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you see anyone there who was detained in the month of May?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In May, on the 21st of May, I saw two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Could you tell us who it was that you saw?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their names I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was there anything that you did know about them, if not their names?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two persons on the 21st of May in the morning, that day that I participated in the front fighting where a friend of mine got killed, I saw them earlier. They said that they were Roma or Gypsy - this is what is what we say - they suspected them of something. I didn't see them anymore that day and I wasn't interested in them. When we returned on the same day in the evening, I know that I saw them in that part that was covered, it was lam [phoen], we called it, like a stable. They were tied with a wire and I know that they were son-in-law and father-in-law. That is, they were in-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just to clarify, when you say that you saw them in that part that was covered, is that a part of the barracks in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you tell us that they suspected them of something, who is the "they"? Who suspected these two persons of something?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that they were tied up means that they were suspected of one thing or another. I can't tell you who suspected of them, because I didn't know who brought them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about what it was that they were suspected of?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was the physical condition of these two people when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't describe that. I can't describe it in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know what ultimately happened to those two persons?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do know that Lahija, my first leader, said that I will sent them to Drenica. I heard him say that. I don't know -- remember with whom he was talking when I heard that. At that time, these words, meaning if you send somebody to Drenica, you will see the end of that person. That person was supposed to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you specifically that that's what that phrase meant?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a phrase that was constantly used that. Was the meaning of that phrase that I knew. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, was there somebody else at that barracks at some point that was detained, someone that you knew from before?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two persons. I met them when I was coming from Albania. I don't know exactly at what time I met them. It might have been the beginning of July or the mid-July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of those two persons?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what are those name, please. We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Pal Krasniqi from Kline and Skender Kugi from a village close by to the village that I come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was the physical condition of those two persons when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day I stopped before the door, I was with a group of friends. They were from Drini Valley. Most of them were Catholics some of them I knew from before. We were returning from Albania. We stopped there because I used to go to that headquarters to meet some friends. When we went inside I saw those two persons. Lahi had told me, Do you know them? Do you know your neighbour? I said, Yes, what has he done, why is he here, I said. You -- you don't know that he was a big fish, meaning a big spy. This is how I understood the word to mean. He said, he has worked for UBD, Yugoslavia secret service and then I asked, I asked I talked with Pal because his brother is a friend of mine, even today. And for the sake of his brother, I asked him he said, I don't know why I'm here. I came here to enlist to become a KLA soldier. I stayed as a soldier for one week and then they suspected me to be a spy and they brought me here, he told me. I saw it with my own eyes. He was maltreated. He was reading a book that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you say he was maltreated could you explain briefly how he looked?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to put it. Somebody beats you, you can see the marks of the beating. You can always tell when somebody is badly beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did either of these two persons say anything to you about the accusations against them, that they were a spy, or a big spy?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't tell me anything. Pal told me that. After Lahi left together with Bandash. I don't know his true name even now. I asked Pal myself. I told him Pal tell me, why are you here, what have you done? He said, They have maltreated me greatly. They forced me to admit to them that an inspector from Peja sent me to get information from KLA. He said, Then I accept it because they were beating me and I said Yes, and I said to him You shouldn't have accepted this but I understand what it means to -- when you are forced to admit something, because I tried it on my own back at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear when you say he told you that he had been forced to admit that an inspector had sent him to get information about the KLA, and inspector for whom?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an inspector from Peja. His name was Aca. Almost everybody in Peja knew that person. An inspector is somebody who is supposed to capture people who commit a theft or rob something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just to be clear, this is -- who does this inspector work for?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked for the Serb service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you explain, if you know, what ultimately happened to Skender Kugi and Pal Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left them the day, I went towards Malisevo. It was July. This is what I remember, if I am not wrong even though much time was elapsed. Then we arrived in Drenica and towards Likovc there are several villages there. Isdrime [phoen] was the last point. When you come from Kline and between Kline and Istog then we went in that direction right at Drenace village. Then I borrowed a car from a friend and we drove -- all over those villages to arrive at the village where my family lives. I met my relatives and I told my uncle about these two persons whom he too knew. I told him they were suspected of being collaborators, of being spies. My uncle said I don't believe that, because -- we were talking more about Skender because he said Skender was a person whom he knew, and there were many persons -- there were certificates to prove that he sent foodstuffs to the KLA, food provisions. And my uncle said, I don't believe that, because he will to work with the Serbs. He had to get commodities, goods from them. But I don't think he has -- he is a spy, so he told me. If you can do something about him, please do that, to save him.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Pal. After the offensive, after the attacks, I heard that -- it was September -- I don't know what happened to them after that. I met his brother after the war. He said I don't know, his

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: with him I told him -- I went to KLA that he had no heard about him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And after -- after Skender died, do you know what happened to the body?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was buried nearby. There was a building meant to be an ambulance it was not finished yet. He was buried behind that building. I heard that his family tried to find out about him. They wanted to take away his body from that place. Somebody in Jablanice told me that they took him to another place where some relatives of his were living. This is what I heard. I didn't see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know where he was ultimately buried?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought first he was buried in Jablanice. Then his body was buried in Irzniq. Some soldiers accompanied him. I don't know where. This is what I heard, that he was buried in Irzniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this in Jablanice. From some friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you say some soldiers accompanied him, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard. This is what I heard, I'm saying. That some soldiers accompanied him and that he was buried with military honours. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you speak to anyone about the fact that you had heard that he had been buried with military honours?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked with Lahi about that. Asked him, I told him that I have heard that he was buried with military honours. I remember you telling me that he is a spy. And you -- how come you didn't know him even though he was your neighbour? He said, Forget about that. These are rumours. So I didn't pursue it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you mentioned Lahi and you mentioned him a couple of other times. When you mention Lahi, is that the same person? I'm sorry, let me ask this first. Who is Lahi when you talk about him here?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lahi is the same person that I have been mentioning all over here, in my statement. His name is Lahi Ibrahimaj. His pseudonym was Magjupi first. That is the person that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you say that Lahi told you that these are rumours what was he talking about? They were rumours that he was a spy or there were rumours that he was buried with military honours?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant that they were words. Words he meant, the military honours. He said, Forget about them that is not true. This is what the implication of his word. That was the answer to my question, when I asked him, that I heard that he was buried with military honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, apart from the persons that you have named, if you could just answer yes or no to this question. Did you see other persons being detained at Jablanica in that barracks?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You've mentioned -- some of the people you have mentioned have been -- you mentioned that they showed signs of being beaten. Did you actually yourself see these people, these detainees being beaten?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just from what you've seen, could you name some of the people that you saw carrying out these beatings, if you know their names? And bearing in mind we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me Your Honour, I'm going to at this point interpose an observation. Which I think is more than just being on -- it's Monday I had had some rest over the weekend. But this entire line of questioning is outside the matters charged in our indictment, it deals with an entirely different geographical area. Deals with an entirely different participants. I believe I understand some of the reason why the Prosecution may be seeking this testimony. However, they are in a better position than I, of course, to explain that to the Court if need be. But with regard to the last question asked which is the names of people, unless those names are in some way connected to people who are on trial here, I think that it stretches the bound the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe Mr. Guy-Smith anticipated my response, which is that these -- these events do go to the widespread or systematic nature of these incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: With regard to the names I would submit that the names of these persons engaged in these beatings go to first of all, completeness of the story. And secondly, they go to some indication of the nature of this widespread and systematic event. In other words, and I don't wish to anticipate too much the witness's testimony on this point, but the persons who are involved in it, the persons who is are involved in the direct beatings do reflect the manner in which these incidents were carried out in this particular place, and we would submit that is this a as spent of the widespread and systematic nature of these crimes which is relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Shin. The decision is that there is a potential relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, bearing in mind that we are in private session, of the beatings that you saw yourself now, that yourself saw, can you name some of these -- can you name the persons that you saw carrying out those beatings?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I give these names, is it possible to make an explanation? I think it is useful to the Court and to the counsel as well. If I'm allowed to make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, if you could please try answering the question first and then provided an explanation. Could we do it that way?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Lahi Ibrahimaj, when he beat Jah Bushati which I didn't mention. I saw Togeri. Idriz Bala was his name. I learned it later. In the beginning nobody knew it. He came to the Jablanica headquarters. Anybody he found he would beat them. I saw Bandashi. The same thing. I could say the same thing about him as well. I saw Muftari and from what I know he was the person that took Jah Bushati and brought him to the headquarters. And another one Xhevdeti, he was from Jablanica. I saw him once. I did not see him the same as the other people in the sense that...

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you wish to provide an explanation to that now?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I'm allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead. Please go ahead and provide an explanation of your answer.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to be here and testify. I am an Albanian; that's what I think, at least. But there are people who are in a more difficult position than me because -- because they have been accused. The people that I mentioned earlier and people of the same -- of the same ilk, they have called me a traitor. Well, I've been in prison in Nis for three months and three days.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Imprisonment was for three years and three months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for a private session here, because there are many criminals at large in Kosovo now. They have killed many people during the war and after the war as well. It was a very difficult situation after the war. I have had threats, there have been threats to my family, to my father --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I apologise for interpreting up the witness. And I know we are all very grateful that he has come to come to the Court to give his evidence and for Your Honours to assist that. But Your Honours, there is a difference between explaining testimony and going on a detour about matter about which in fact have not been raised in examination-in-chief and I would ask Your Honours to -- exclude the witness commenting on matters which have not in fact been sought to be elicited in examination-in-chief. By all means, an explanation in relation to evidence but not in relation to collateral matters which need not engage your Your Honours’ time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan for having concern at the time but in the personal and political circumstance, think in fairness to the witness, he should be allowed to express these matters that concern him deeply about his evidence. If there is more that you wish to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't want to take too much of your time myself. But these are many things that have followed me all the time, from the time of the war, in the prison, and now as well. And it's been very difficult for me to come here and give evidence. And that's why I have asked for it to be a private session. It's because of my family, of my relatives. There are many people who don't know about the things that have happened. Many people have been killed after the war in Kosovo. They were innocent, they were killed only because they believed in one party or another party. I don't belong to any party, but I never said things that did not exist or did not happen, although I have been called a traitor. Those people can well remain there where they are in their lofty positions as patriots, while I am here. This is an international court. This is not a court about Serbia as it's been called in Kosovo. And that's why I would like to apologise if I make any mistakes or give inaccurate dates because it's been a long time and I can't remember all of the things as they happened and I'm very excited and nervous at this moment. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. To the best of your knowledge what was Lahi Ibrahimaj's position at Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: At his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry my question may have come unclear. What was his -- what was his position within the KLA at Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning when I went to Jablanica, he was a commander. I can corroborate that with another fact. Because at the moment I went there to the barracks from the headquarters -- the headquarters was Lahi's house -- when I was sent to be admitted as a soldier. I met Leopardi. He admitted me as a soldier. He accepted me there. But how I knew that Lahi was a commander. This was because many people from the village came, some in uniform, some without a uniform, they came from various villages, and there was a list that he made that he put -- posted at the gate of the barracks and this list described the people who had the right to go inside the barracks and the first name there was Lahi Ibrahimaj's name. There was were other names as well but this is the fact that showed me that he was the leader there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: As far as you know, was there anyone in a more senior position to Lahi Ibrahimaj in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Very briefly on Jah Bushati. Was he -- just to confirm: Was he a detainee at Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said it earlier. Jah Bushati was stopped by Muftari. He was traveling from Kosarice to Dukagjin in the direction of Jablanica. There is a hill there. There is a river as well the Betonaj River [phoen] and he was stopped on the way. Muftari brought him to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know why -- do you know why Jah Bushati was stopped and why he was brought to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say anything concrete about this. He was stopped because he had done some spy work. A day or two before that, somebody had been shot. This person was with his brother and his brother escaped. This was a person call the Shala from Buqan. But I don't know, I can't -- maybe his surname, I can't give you his surname. So one of them was killed and the other injured. And later, in Jablanica, I heard that Jaha had something to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, was there a time in 1998 when you left Jablanica and did not return?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when was that, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Maybe by the end of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And bearing in mind that we are in private session, could you explain briefly why it was that you left?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief. There were around 76 soldiers, 76 of us in the headquarters, in Jablanica. Maybe not the headquarters but the barracks where the soldiers stayed. After we had some kind of counting of the soldiers, and I know that we had lunch, I had to go to the point together with my -- two of my uncle's sons, together with which I was a soldier. Jaha and Brahimi [as interpreted]. Jaha was killed by the Serbs on the 22nd of October, 1998. Bashkim was wounded on his head. And because of the wound, he cannot see now, and he has a lot of problems with his brain, his mind. They went to the point while Mala stopped me. He told me that you have to do a very important job. He gave me a revolver, a Croatian type, 15, number 15, and he told me you have to kill Rrok Berisha tonight. I asked why, and he said, this offensive that happened in Luga e Baranit is because of him. I took the gun. I went to Jaha and Bashtimi. I told them, This is what happened to me, I have been given this order. Jaha could not believe me. He said, you are joking. This is not -- this cannot be true. And I told him, Yes, this is true, I'm telling you. He said if I knew that these things happened within the KLA, I would not join. We stayed there for half an hour, or an hour, I'm not sure how long. I was thinking about what I would do, and I told Jaha I want to go and see whether this person looks like. During that conversation, Jaha told me and my family told me that our families have this traditional and we know each other because we lived in the Zhabel village. My father was born there. There is in the Gjakova municipality, close to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you please do not mention the name of your home village and there is no need to mention the names of your cousins either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And Your Honours out of an abundance of caution have the names of his cousins redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, sorry to interrupt you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was told by my family that his family was a very good one and a loyal one. I mean the family of the person. I knew that he was an activist in the LDK. He had also been a member of the human rights organisation or association. I went to his door, and called out his name. He came out. I started to talk with him. I told him who I was, and I told him why I was there. He said No problem. Well, if it's worth it, you can kill me, if you think it's worth it. And I said no, I have come here to ask you, is there anything bad, is there anything wrong between you and the leaders? And he said, No, I have been on very good terms, especially with Ramush Haradinaj. We had a meeting in my room, in my soba [phoen], when both sides came together. That's what they referred to. It was the Tahir Zemi side and Ramush Haradinaj side. So they had supper here. We had very good relations, both with Tahir and Ramush. And he said, Only when they came in Gllogjan we exchanged some words with regard to the population. Only that. I don't know of anything else. If you want me to speak more at length about this case...

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, if you could just -- just say was it -- my question had been to you why you had left Jablanica without returning. Was this the reason, this assignment that you had been given, was this the reason that you had left?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: To come to the reason why I left, I made another appointment with that person later that night, so I met him again. Both of us knew that or believed that people were being killed. Innocent people were being killed for personal interests of people. People who were within the KLA. And I said to him, If you can influence leaders of the KLA or people who the Kosovan people trust, and I said, If you want me -- if you want me to escort you to take you to another place to be safe I can do that. He said no, no, there is no need for that. So we had that appointment again with him. I sent word to my leader, the one who gave me that gun, and I said to him, Take your gun back and we will see each other later, again. So I went back home. I spoke to my family and they told me, No, you can't do these things, if somebody tells you to kill another person without any fact or any trial or anything like that. I stayed for some days at home. I was ready to go back, but some relatives came to me and mentioned that case, and asked me -- and they said How could you, how Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could you do that? How were you -- how could you be prepared to kill Rrok Berisha and I was surprised, how could people know about that thing. So I went back home and I waited until October. There was a person who came from Montenegro with many people from there, and I wrote a letter. I sent it to Ramush Haradinaj. He responded to me through relatives - I don't want to give names - the response was that I don't know about these things. I'm not aware. I have kept that letter at home. He said I'm not aware about these things. I knew these as strong soldiers. Many other good words. And he said you can come back, I can place you here or somewhere else if you want. But it was a very turbulent time. OSCE was there. There was a cease-fire between the KLA and the Serbs. We were waiting during those days. A neighbour came to me during those days, and he spoke of similar cases that had happened to him. We had many plans to go to Rugova or to go to Albania where people were being trained. That's what we had heard. It was close to the new year. We had prepared some winter clothes when they came at about 5.00 in the morning. We were surrounded. The Serb forces surrounded us --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... break that. Your Honours, I'm not sure if that is a suitable time to break. I'm sorry, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because of our disrupted starting time I am contemplating this session ending at about 20 minutes to which will be the limit of our tapes and having only one break. So carry on for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, sorry to have interpreted you. I think for this we can go into open session, but just before we do, can I just one clarification. You had mentioned that your cousin had been shot and the translation claim through as 22nd of October 1998. Is that date correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the 22nd of December when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just one more question in closed session before we go to open. You mentioned -- you testified that you were in prison for three and a half years. Could you tell us when it was that you were released?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was released on the 26th of March. I was transferred -- transferred to the Dubrava prison and on it's 27th of March, I was released. There was this agreement between Steiner and the leadership of Kosovo and Batic, from Serbia. I don't know who else it was that they had the agreement with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could go back into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before then, could you determine when it was that he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please give us the date that you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: 22nd of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you say you were released on the 27th of March, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was released on the 27th of March 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. A quick observation: The witness's answer commencing on page 26, line 10 and concluding at page 30, line 10, deals with matters that I believe are outside of the geographic and temporal bounds of the indictment, a matter that we have raised on previous occasions, and would object to the answer and the information contained therein on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is noted, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, without mentioning the specific dates or the name of the place, could you tell us what happened when the Serb forces came to your village?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around 5.00 in the morning. The neighbours close to us, next door, they told us that they had heard noises, noises, cars sometime that morning. We were -- I was in my room on the first floor of the house. There was only one room in that -- on that floor. When I got up, I saw the police in the yard. I saw my father in the yard. I saw them going into my uncle's house, breaking -- smashing the windows, and I did not know what to do. We had some guns that we had hidden in my uncle's -- my uncle's son's house. There were many. We had -- there were many people there. There were around 50.000 people in the place where I lived, in the village where I lived, together with my relatives. I just put on my trousers and I sat down there. They came into the room with their guns. They tied me and they threw me to the floor just like many other people. The OSCE came, there were many policemen in the room. I was tried to hide from them. I don't know for how long I was lying there. There was this big arm chair that was on -- placed over my head. Then I was taken outside, placed against the wall. I saw my uncle's son there as well. He was also tied. And the same -- the same thing happened again there. We were hit several times. We were taken into a police Jeep. On the way to Peja we were stopped and taken out of the Jeep and into a Zastava-type vehicle. There were some civilians in that car and they asked me questions, were you a soldier? And I said yes. And I know that they hit me several times. I was covered in blood. From Tuesday, then it was Friday in the evening that they were taken to the prison, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, where were you first taken?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the prison in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now the persons in your home village who came to get you, you said they hit you. Just to be clear. What do you mean by they? Who are they?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs, the policemen. There were civilians as well, but they were all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you taken somewhere after you were the Peja police station?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Peja prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And after that were you taken somewhere?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed for some time in the Peja prison. But on the 3rd of May, 1998, we were transferred to the Dubrava prison in a bus. This was in 1999. There were people in that bus with their arms broken, with their skull open. We were take be to the Dubrava prison. They called me and two other people from my family, and they told us to step aside. We stayed there in that prison until the 19th of May. NATO bombed on the 19th of May, Pavilion C where I was, and my uncle's son came to the cell door and he said I think we are going to be free. It was very difficult to open that door. The guards had all left. There were no guards, only prisoners in the prison. There were some old people, elderly people, and also people who had stayed there for a long time, people who had committed crimes or people like us who were called terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness, sorry to interrupt you there, just to be clear: Who was calling you a terrorist at that point?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs, the guards in the prison. We were all terrorists for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And after you had been at this prison, were you then taken somewhere else? And please don't mention the specific date of your transfer if there was a transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in a motive of assisting my learned friend and hopefully that he can achieve his target of five more minutes, I'm quite content for the witness to be let on all these issues. They are not a matter of dispute between the parties and may save court time and it may assist my friend to get things moving faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Witness could you please mention the name of the prison you were taken to next, from the prison?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 10th of June -- from the 24th of May to the 10th of June, we were transferred to Lipjan. On the 10th of June, in the morning, again, we were taken in buses to Serbia, all of us. I was lucky to remain in Nis together with my uncle. My uncle's son was taken to Pograxhe although he was wounded. I don't know where they took the other people. Pograxhe, Sem [phoen], Belgrade and other prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And witness, when you were originally arrested by the Serbian forces you say that you were beaten. Have you recovered fully from those beatings?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never stopped. I thought that maybe after the investigation, after I went to prison it would be easier for me. That they would go easier on me. But it happened in the prison as well. But when the bombing, the bombing started, we did not even have bread to eat. We were beaten daily inside there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Witness, how is your physical condition now? Are there any injuries still remaining from those beatings?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't been to the doctor, to have a check-up or anything. I have been a sports person before. Before the Milosevic regime [as interpreted] it was easier for us. We had good food, we had the right to go out in the yard in the prison and walk a little bit. We could do some exercises, physical exercises, and there was enough food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. We will have a break now and resume at 10 minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin. Before that happens, I understand that is a matter of interpretation to be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would like to make a correction. It was before we broke last session. It was said, if I can find it on the transcript. I said "before the Milosevic regime"; it should be "after Milosevic fell".

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It's page 35 at the very end of page 34 and page 35, lines 1 and 2. Line 1, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for making that correction. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And Your Honours, the Prosecution had no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it please Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Karim Kahn along with lead counsel Michael Mansfield we represent Fatmir Limaj who sits behind us. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now hopefully you will be pleased to know, no doubt, that we don't intent to detain you too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be of some assistance if I very briefly detail the areas that I intend to ask questions about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And witness, they surround your initial joining of the KLA. I will then ask you some questions about your alleged meeting with Commander Celiku in Klecka. What I'm not going to ask you any questions about is anything about Jablanica, simply because we don't know anything about that. And that's the reason why -- while whilst not accepting what you say, we're not going to ask you questions. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Simply, we don't know what happened. Now, Witness, it's correct, isn't it, that you joined the Kosovo Liberation Army when you were 21 years of age. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And at the time you joined, you had no previous military experience; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And I think you explained to Their Honours that the first training you had was about a month after you first joined the Kosovo Liberation Army in the middle of May 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said from mid-April to mid-May. This is how long the exercise or the training lasted. But even before that, I took part in the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you remember saying yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And Your Honours, it's LiveNote page 21, line 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you remember saying yesterday, when you were asked about training that the training occurred "sometime in mid-May after I had started to participate in other fronts as well." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: First you said yesterday. Yesterday I didn't say anything. Secondly, I didn't start in the middle of May, but I am repeating it. The training started in the middle of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, you're quite correct. Thank you for correcting me, I do appreciate it. I meant, of course, on Friday before we broke up. You said that the training occurred in mid-May "after I started to participate in other fronts as well." Do you remember saying that as well or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am repeating. I didn't start, that the training started in mid-May. It did start in mid-April. Maybe it's a mistake of translation or some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: But the training started after you joined the KLA, and started after you had engaged in operations. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And the training that you were given by the KLA, that took place in the village -- in the villages where were you were based; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In those villages, and around those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: There was no special KLA training centre, was there?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me there, in that place or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In the place where you started your training, you say now in the middle of April.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some special places for that. But in the village, in the village where I was based, and in the -- other villages there were some fields, pastures, gorges or parts of mountains where we were trained in different military exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from these fields and gorges, there was no special centre with special facilities, specifically focused on training a new army. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the school of Zhabel village, a village near Jablanice, there was a shooting ground which we ourselves built to be more or less in conformity with the standards of the western armies. That was also a place where we could exercise and train ourselves together with other villagers. It was in the courtyard of the school of Zhabel village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And there was a huge problem of shortage of weapons when you joined the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I think, for example, you yourself were given a somewhat of an antique, old Russian rifle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And many of your comrades had old rifles and old hunting rifles. It wasn't the best and most modern equipment, was it. People found and used what they could.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did use those kind of weapons that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And because people and many of your comrades that you spoke to joined for exactly the same reason that you had joined, in that you had enough of this lengthy period of Serb domination, discrimination and persecution and you decided that the only way you would get liberty was to fight for your rights. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But at the time this was what I thought and that's why I did what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Just going back to training. You were never given any lectures on the 1994 Geneva Conventions or the Protocols Additional thereto, or The Hague Regulations, were you? It was very basic, crawling and climbing and shooting your old weapons. But you weren't given lessons on the laws of war, were you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not. They taught us how to shoot with a gun, but maybe I didn't get you right in when you mention those conventions and regulations. Nobody taught us anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You did get me right, thank you. And there was no discussion about strategy or larger questions of the operation of a military machine, was there?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember anyone telling us anything about the strategy. I know that when I went to Albania to get arms, some people used -- learned to use heavy arms like artillery or grenade-launchers. In those places where some people were located, those people who received the people that went there to get arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, you say that the second occasion that you saw Celiku was when you went to Klecka. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And that was the day that Klecka was attacked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understand attack is rather different. I see it in -- two different points of view. There were many please in Kosova that were shelled now and again. You might call that attack. That night that I told -- spoke here about there was a shelling. But the attack with infantry troops, if it happened it didn't happen on that day that I was there. It might have taken place on another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You remember giving a statement to the Prosecution in October 2004, do you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And that statement was read back to you and you signed that statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And do you remember telling the Prosecution in that statement that after your second meeting with Celiku, and for my learned friends it's page 53 of the October statement, that night Klecka attack happened. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said it even a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Klecka attack in fact happened on the 25th to 26th of August, 1998? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you say that Klecka -- do you know when Klecka fell?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know if it fell on the day that you left Klecka? Could that be possible or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that even that day it was attacked on the next day too, but when it fell is I don't know [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you had been in Berisa I think three or four days before your second meeting with Celiku. Is that correct, or have I got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I may have said two or three day, but I wasn't sure. Much time has passed. I have moved about a lot, so I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course. We understand we're asking to recollect events that happened many years ago, so please do take your time.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You had been sent to Berisa by your unit commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And because of an order given to you by your unit commander, you went to Berisa, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was with us, but I don't know whether he came up to Berisa or whether he turned or came halfway. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, you say that the first time that you saw Celiku was on the day or maybe the day after you arrived Berisa. That's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And I think you say that what Celiku told you was simply if you need help you can ask for help from Klecka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you ask the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course. You say that in your conversation with Celiku he said that you were acting in place of a missing commander and also that if there was anything -- if you needed anything, you should contact Klecka and get some help. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that you are a commander. I understand it differently. He said you will be responsible for this unit for the time that the commander is away. And that if you need something, that is, if you need some clothes or some equipment or so on, you can come to Klecke. Was a person from the village. He had a car of Lada make and he was in a way as if designated. To my recollection his name was Sadik he was wearing a moustache then. He saw him several times. I didn't mention this before in my statement. His duty was that if I needed something, he should take me to Klecke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: When you arrived in Berisa, is it fair to say to that things were somewhat chaotic because of the ongoing Serbian offensive that had started?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that it may have been like that. I don't remember well whether the meeting was that day or on the next day, but I remember that in the evening we were on a hill. It might have been that night or the next night. From there, we could see many villages, Arlat and other villages which were burning. We could see the flames from there and the fields around from Arlat along the road to Malisevo. Everything was burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And aside from all of the burning you could see, it's right, isn't it, that the KLA from your experience was feeling extremely stretched and disorganised because of the summer offensive that had started. Is that fair or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been disorganised in some places. In some places there were shortages of munitions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In total you were in Berisha for about three or four days. Would it be fair to say that in fact you were not very familiar with the area around Berisa, having been previously based in Jablanica. Is my assessment fair?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was three or four days. I can't tell you for sure how long I stayed. And you are right when you say that I was not very familiar with that region; I said this on Friday. I knew all of the villages near that area were called the Berisa villages. I might have been wrong, but that was what I believed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I think in your evidence on Friday you described various zones of operation. For example, the Dukagjini -- the Dukagjini zone and other zones. You had heard those names before, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And this area around Klecka, you described that as the Berisa area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And this territory this zone that you say existed called Berisa --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sorry, I think that's maybe misstating the evidence. I don't believe the witness ever said that there was a zone called the Berisa zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to page 35 of LiveNote of yesterday. Line 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Friday, once again my mistake. Berisa was the name of the whole territory. But, Your Honour, I could clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand stood that to be speaking of geographic area rather than a particular zone. But to clarify it, I'm sure would be helpful for all of us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, what area that zone came under?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to interrupt. If perhaps there could be some more clarity about what zone we're speaking about when we say "that zone" and what area that zone came under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you wouldn't mind I think it would be helpful to make it a little more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You say, Witness, that you went to Berisa. And you say that that area was under Celiku. Do you know, according to you, what zone that area was in?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used this on Friday. I spoke about zones or territories or -- I don't know how to put it. And I said that I mentioned which leader was responsible for that zone. When we talk about Celiku's zone, I said that it had -- it comprised some villages around Malisevo or each beyond Malisevo. In the Kline municipality I also said a that if we look at Berisa only as a zone, meaning the place where I was based, this is what I knew it to be.
