Regarding Celiku's zone, I said it comprises a part in the -- in the vicinity of Malisevo, Pristina-Peja asphalt road on one side and on the other side I thought it comprised Orahovac municipality, Suva Reka municipality, because I knew who was operating where. Maybe I was not very precise, and I'm not saying that everything I know now I told here what I knew then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, no doubt it's my fault. But if you remember on Friday you talked about Ramush Haradinaj being the zone commander of Dukagjini. You talk about Sylejman Salimi being in charge of Krasniqi and you talk about Remi being in charge of Llap. Do you remember saying that on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again, but I believe that is misstating the evidence. If my learned colleague is referring to page 40 of the transcript, while the Dukagjini zone is named, there is no reference specifically to the names -- I believe the two names were Pastrik possibly and Llap. I'm sorry, it's not clear on the LiveNote just now but I don't believe there is a reference to the names of those zones there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that wasn't mentioned on Friday and that's exactly the thrust of my cross-examination. So I would ask my friend to be somewhat hesitant. Of course he does say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, you started off to try and find out about the Berisa area and what zone. I think we've lost that thought somewhere along the road. Do you want to get back to that and clear that up at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: What zone do you say Celiku was in charge of?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said even earlier, from Klecke. At least this is what I knew it to be. The villages of Divlak, Novoselle, I thought that these villages were under Celiku's control. Terpeze, Malisevo, even beyond Malisevo. I repeated it several times. I said it comprises a village of Orahovac, Suhareke municipalities, and on the side of the asphalt road to Pristina. This is what I believed. I think that my answer is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the name of that zone or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew it to be -- as Celiku's zone, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And not knowing the name of the zone, in fact you didn't -- you don't know who was the commander of Lapusnik, do you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said anything regarding Lapusnik's commander. I'm putting it to you again. That this is what I knew then. I repeated it several times. That was my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And had you no idea not knowing the identity of that commander of Lapusnik whether or not he was a superior or subordinate or an equal to Celiku; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question I'm afraid. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You have no idea, do you, Witness, as to the identity of the commander of Lapusnik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I already -- I already said and knew I have told you, and I am repeating that as far as I knew, Celiku was the commander of that zone. And the way I saw it was as Celiku's zone and not by any other name, not like Ramush zone, like Dukagjin zone. So these were zones or places which were very small in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And you don't know exactly how small Celiku's zone was, do you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know how small or how big it was. I knew as I already described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And what you had picked up was largely based upon gossip and rumour and what your general impression was in those few days that you were in Berisa; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before going to Berisa, I had been in that area many times. I have heard from other soldiers, soldiers that I knew, some of them were my friends. A friend of mine was in Jablanica. I don't know -- I don't like to mention his name. I knew his pseudonym. He was in Celiku's zone, and I have met that person in Terpeze.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And in fact you said on Friday that you got information about the commanders and their zones because information was transmitted and broadcast through television and radio stations. Am I right that the information you got from television was received after the war?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding this information, that is, Celiku was a commander, I didn't learn that after the war. It was given also during the war. But I -- to stress my point, I said that I heard other soldiers speaking of as such. But I also heard it through the radio stations, the television and other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And just for the sake of clarity, you said on Friday that Celiku did not introduce himself but you became aware of his name later; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the true name or the pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The real name of Celiku.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the real name of Celiku I learned later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: That was after the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure. It is possible that it was after the war. I can't tell you exactly when. It was maybe after the war, because I was in gaol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that you became aware of his name perhaps at the same time that you became aware of Qerqiz's name once you heard the indictment and heard the TV reports and after their arrest and being sent over to The Hague. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is possible regarding Qerqiz, meaning that I learned this much later. After the indictment made public or so. But regarding Celiku I knew when I was in gaol, because we talked when we were in gaol with other friends. His brother. We were together with his brother. And he came several times to my room and I went to his room several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And the brother that was -- of Mr. Limaj that was in prison with you, that was Dimir Limaj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You never heard of a prison or a place where people were being detained in Lapusnik at the time that you were in Berisa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't hear about that prison then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much. I'm sorry that I have taken slightly longer than I intended but hopefully you won't be too much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm happy to commence, but Mr. Shin is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just if we could please have a redaction from line 18 through 21, I believe. Yes. Sorry, down to 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber having great difficulty today because our page numbering doesn't seem to accord with that of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It's -- if we could go briefly in private session I will indicate what lines that is a little more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private. 14 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- I believe it is it page 48, line 18 or maybe just before on the previous line when it's sentence begins: "But regarding Celiku I knew because we talked" -- from there and then down to the last reference to his brother, which would take us down to line 24, where the answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the reference to Celiku going to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour is entirely correct. If we could begin with "His brother" on line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And is that simply because they were together in a place?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well perhaps out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll go to open session now and then Mr. Guy-Smith who's been waiting anxiously in the wings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. How are you doing? Are you all right?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm doing right -- very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A moment ago you were speaking about such things as ammunition and it's fair to say that during the entire time that you were fighting there was always a shortage of ammunition, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there were shortages in some places, but not everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where you were, there was a shortage there, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in many places. Which place to you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, starting at the beginning when you joined the KLA and you were handed that old Russian sniper's rifle. At that point in time. You didn't have a lot of ammunition with you, did you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first went there and got that weapon, I had munitions for that. They gave the munition along with the weapon to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How many rounds did you have?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count the bullets but I had plenty of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And did there come a time that you ran out of rounds from the firing that you did?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: That weapon was given to me when I was admitted to the KLA and I used it for a few days during the training. Then I changed it with another friend with Leopardi -- after asking Leopard. And then I got a Kalashnikov which was taken from Albanian. And I had a bag full of munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you needed further munitions, how did you get that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have any specific occasion in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the first time you ran out of munitions when you were using your Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never ran out of munitions personally. Because I went often to Albania and therefore I had plenty of munitions for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How many times did you go to Albania during the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that you went often, would that be more than ten times?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, less than ten times. Seven or eight. I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you went to Albania, could you tell us of the first time that you went to Albania, how long you were gone from Kosova?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I went, I think I have mentioned it already, we travelled during the night -- in the evening and during the night. And it was sometime in the morning when we arrived in Prac village which was known in Kosova as a place called Kulle e Sali Berishes the tower of Sali Berishes. It is possible that we rested for a while and in the evening we returned in -- to Kosovo again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that the other six or seven times that you went to Albania you spent approximately the same amount of time out of Kosovo, maybe a day or a night or two at the most. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one instance when we went the purpose was to get arms for a territory from Kline up to Istok whose population is mostly Catholics. We went there two times. The first time I went with some friends. We didn't find the weapons we were looking for so we didn't get many weapons. We got only a few of them. So together with some friends we

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: arms to bring to Kosova. These lasted maybe a week or two weeks, until he came, until we came back. And I know that when we came back, we fell in an ambush at Rrasa e Zogut. There was fighting. One was killed, Kole Mirdita was the name, from Drenas village up near Klina. And unfortunately, we got along very few weapons, only those we were carrying on our shoulders and a friend was injured. The others we left there, at the border, the other weapons. That was maybe the longest time we spent in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour I believe there is a need for some redaction based upon witness's last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's of any assistance, if it could be from line 12 through line 14, that sentence. So after the word Tirana, the sentence that appears after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That enough? Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could just have a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I think that should be sufficient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've indicated that you travelled in a fair number of different areas in Kosovo and my question is now directed to whether or not you can help us and identify for us whether or not there were any medical clinics in the zones that you have discussed with us thus far. And I take it you have the zones in mind, but that would the Llap zone, the Pastrik zone and Dukagjin.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Llap or about Pastrik. I know about Dukagjin plateau. I know because it was there when I went to become a soldier. There was an ambulance there to treat two or three injured. There was also one in Irzniq village near Gllogjan. After that instance when my friend was injured that I mentioned earlier, there was another village near Gllogjan in Gramacel. There was fighting there and two other people were injured and we took them to Irzniq, to that hospital that is I knew it. And on the next day we got them back to the territory from where we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question in another area. You had mentioned that at one point you were in a prison which was the Dubrova [sic] prison. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While you were in that prison, I take it you saw a fair number of your fellow Albanians also at that prison. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mainly most of them were Albanians with few exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As you sit here today, can you tell us about how many Albanian prisoners you saw at Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the day of the bombing. I knew very few of them because I was in the isolation. After the air strikes we came out in the yard of the prison. Then I saw many Albanians. But I can't tell you exactly how many. They -- they said then and even now that as much as we could count with our friends there were about 1.000 persons detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the Serbs massacred a fair number of Albanians at the Dubrava prison. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They say that there are about 200 people killed altogether by NATO and the Serbs. But from what we would gather there were about 18 killed from NATO, and about 170 or more were killed by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say 170 or more were killed by the Serbs, were those people summarily executed, shot?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first day of the air strike, only three persons were killed. And the Serbs used that. They through bombs, killed detainees with snipers from the surrounding walls. I can cite two instances that I witnessed myself. Once was when they told us to go near to the wall where there was a corner, two walls met there, there was a border as if they wanted to count them, us. The same person who called us as if to count us because he said we will transfer to you another prison, he fired at us with a hand mortar. And then fired at with us an automatic gun. And they threw hand-grenades from both side of the walls at us. There were many people killed and many injured. Whoever could flee fled. We tried to find refuge in the cellar or some trenches or canals. After one or two days, I think it was on the 23rd, we entered a cellar. In the evening, we cooked some pancakes. We ate them because we were very hungry. On the next morning when the day dawned, I saw them entering the place wearing masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say you saw "them" entering the place wearing masks are you referring to the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb forces. We were about 20 persons hidden in this cellar. And when we saw them entering the cell, they started to fire at us. That cellar had some big cauldrons or some tubes to -- for the hot water that ran -- that was used in the prison. It was very large cellar, like this hall, and so we tried to hide behind those ventilators, cauldrons or tubes. They fired bombs at us -- they through bombs at us from the windows. After ten minute it is was full of smoke. We couldn't see anything. Some of the tubes were broken. Some of the pipes were broken and the water start to the fall and they started to kill people. My cousin was injured because of a bomb and he is blind now because of that injury. And he is not in -- in full possession of his mental faculties. He cannot eat properly. He eats very little. Ten people died. They were lying on the floor. Some of them I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the tragedy that you just described to us is a result of Serbian activity; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May I make it clear that we on behalf of Isak Musliu do not cross-examine on detainees or any issues surrounding this witness's evidence regarding Jablanica, not upon the basis that we accept it but on the basis that we are in the a position to challenge it, our position, in essence, being precisely similar to that of Mr. Limaj. Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private. 11 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sir, I represent Isak Musliu and I first want to ask you one or two questions about your present position. You told us on Friday that you are a serving officer with the KPS and you protect government facilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not -- I work in the Kosova police service, the security division. Which is responsible for government, state, police facilities for the courts and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is that regarded in Kosova as an important possession?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: For that, you have to take a test, a police test. There are some people who examine the test to see whether you meet the criteria of working in that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it regarded as a position that has some prestige in Kosova?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what to say in answer to your question. I may Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say it's regarded with some prestige because in fact there is a great unemployment in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You told us on Friday that you have held this position for about five months. Does it follow from that, that you obtained this position around October of last year?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to school in Vushtrri in September. For two weeks we underwent training. If I'm not mistaken, we started training on the 6th of September, and I think it was on the 21st that we started to work, in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You had been released from four years plus of gaol on about the 27th of March of 2003, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 2002. I saw it on the monitor it was put 2003 but it is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It was put on the monitor because that is what you said. Let's be clear about it: Were you released in March 2002 or March 2003?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You made, didn't you, two statements to the ICTY to this Tribunal, and they are respectively dated dates in October 200, the 21, 22, and the 24th and then another statement on the 8th of December of 2004. Do you agree with those dates?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. October, December. I don't remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: But then you had secured your job in the KPS, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was working...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is there any connection between those two facts?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: What connection do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did the fact that you had given statements to the ICTY investigator in any way in any sense assist you with regard to the prestigious job that you now have in Kosova?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think even earlier. It's not that it is a highly prestigious job, but given the high unemployment rate in Kosova it's not a bad job. When I start to the give the statement I was working even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Had you benefitted from any promotion in your job since giving the statements to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: What benefits do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I think I said: Promotion. Have you received any promotion, improvement in your position?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Finally on this topic and then we should be able to go into open session. Did you approach the Office of the Prosecutor or did they approach you to make statements?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not I who approached them. I think I have mentioned that. But I may repeat it. They asked me to do that. The first time I met them we met in my home. They came to me with a relative of mine and they asked me whether I was willing to make a statement about what I saw in the war, what I had done, about the time I spent in gaol, and so on, and I made the statement that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you how it was they were coming to you for a statement?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A relative of mine who came with them, they called him. I mean they have talked with him. It doesn't interest me what they discussed. They came together and I made the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And finally on this topic, just yes or no, please. Within your knowledge, is this relative of yours also someone who has made a statement to the OTP, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He's a person who -- through whom they came to me. That was the only thing what he did. You asked me how I met with them, and that's why I mentioned that relative of mine, because it was through him that I met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to move on, please, to deal with your dealings as you've described them with the man you knew as Qerqiz. That's what I'm going to deal with now. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Open or...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that can be in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I will repeat that in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm moving on to deal with your dealings with Qerqiz. You told us on Friday of being collected in a car in which there was Qerqizi, which car took you and other man to Klecka. You recall, I expect, telling us all about that on Friday?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I first of all want to see if I understood your evidence as to when this event took place. Just before you described that event to us, you said at page 46 of the transcript for Friday at lines 4 and 5: "It was a time when the Serb forces attacked several points that were controlled by the KLA." And then you went on to describe going to Terpeze and then this collection by car that contained Qerqiz, the dark-red Golf. Can I suggest -- or let me ask you rather than suggest anything: What month of the year was it do you say when this car collected you to take you to Klecka?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if the interpreters could please repeat the answer because it did not appear on the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. I was about to make the same request. It broke up in my ear phones as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could you repeat the month, please, Witness as to when it was that this car collected you to take to you Klecka containing Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the month of July. It is the same time that I was in that area, or that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: On the 25th and 26th of July, as part of the major Serb summer offensive, the village of Lapusnik fell back into Serb hands. Had that happened before you were collected in this car?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have already mentioned that. I am not sure whether it was on the same day, one day after I went to Berisa. The case of the car, that is, when they came with the car, was maybe one or two days after what I said earlier, after this instance. I cannot be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I want you to try to be precise because my difficulty is, you see, is my client has no recollection of this event whatsoever. So I need you to help us when it is you say that alleged event occurred. Now, had Lapusnik fallen or hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must have been after the fall of the Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you have a conversation in a car with Qerqizi, you say, and talked about ordinary matters after they told you that Celiku wanted to talk do you. What ordinary matters did you talk about in this car journey to Klecka?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain it to you briefly. I think I said it on Friday. Usually when people meet we greet each other. We exchange courtesy conversations, how are you, how are you getting on or some minor joke. I can't be precise what we said. It was just a talk, normal conversation between two people who meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You see you could be precise about this when you met with the OTP on the 21st and 22nd of October 2004. Because you were to tell them at paragraph 52 of this statement that you made and signed as being truthful that you got into the car and you were told not to interfere with local affairs which was a reference to an incident involved two young women. Now, did you have a talk about knowing in particular or a problem regarding two young women? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Could the statement be put in front of the witness if he will be cross-examined on the contents thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well the answer is of course it can. I wonder if we could it in a shorthand way first to see if we can save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour, did I interrupt? I can wait for the answer. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Witness, do you accept in a signed statement that you made to the OTP in 2004 you told them that you got into the car and were told not to interfere with local affairs? Do you accept that you said that? If you don't, then I can put the statement in front of you.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't say that we talked about that in the car. I said in the car we talked about normal things. The talk you are referring to occurred after we entered the headquarters. Maybe it is a mistake of translation or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In that case I am going to have put the statement in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I wonder if he may see, please, the Albanian version of the statement that he made dated the 21st, 22nd and 24th of the October.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm assuming it follows the same numbering. First of all by way of identification, Witness, would you be good enough to look at the end of that statement you have been given and see if your signature appears on it above and then below a date of October 2004. No, it's above it. It's the interpreter's signature that's appears below. Is your signature on this statement?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Underneath paragraph 93. Under neat the words "witness acknowledgment." Do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is no signature here but I know it's not a question of signature. I want to hear what I -- or to see what you put to me earlier about that talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may of assistance to Mr. Topolski. It would be the English version that has the signature if that is helpful to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Shin should have stopped me earlier. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to take you right to it, Witness. Paragraph 52, please. Begins with the words "After two or three days." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: "After two or three days, Qerqiz whose name I came to know later to be Isak Musliu came to me with another soldier and told me Celiku had called me. I got into his car and went with him to Celiku." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good. "Initially it was a formal type of conversation. Then he specifically told me not to interfere in local affairs and told me that I was called for a specific job and when I will be needed I will be informed. We had these arguments. I remember Shukri Buja was also present in that room and there was some other soldiers I do not know." So it seems a little confusing, so I need your help. It seems to be that you are saying here that in a car with Qerqizi you were not to interfere with local affairs. Do you remember saying that now?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can repeat it now. It is well written here, after two, three days it means together with another soldier, Qerqiz came and told me that Celiku wanted me. I went in the car and went to Celiku. That is something else. Then there is full stop. Initially it was a formal type of conversation. Then he specifically told me not to interfere in local affairs and told me that I was called for a specific job and when I will be needed I will be informed. There is a full stop. It doesn't specify whether this talk took place. That is why I am here I can explain to you. Even though there are some mistakes of translation, and -- it's a problem one things are translated from one language into another. Because I talked with Qerqiz but with the other person who took me with his car. So that conversation was initially, as I said, a formal one. And then it ended look that. You don't need to deal with that and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You did have a conversation in a car sharing it with Qerqiz, did you? You're absolutely sure about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In light of that answer, yes, I would now like you to see the second version of your Albanian statement dated 8 December 2004, please, and I'd like you to turn to paragraph 20 of it. Again, with the kind help of Mr. Younis. And now I put my thanks to him on record for all to see and hear. Now this is a second statement that you made which is really in the form of questions and answers and I want you first of all to go to paragraph 19 and the question the investigator is asking you is this is it not: When did you first meet Qerqiz. Can you describe how he looked at the time. Do you see that question, paragraph 19?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You never gave an answer to his description but we've leave that for a moment. Let's look at your answer. The first time I met him was when he came to me when I was situated on a hill above Terpeze and told me to follow him to Klecka to meet Commander Celiku. Witness, you were never in a car with Qerqizi, were you?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been in a car with Qerqizi. The reason why I didn't answer the question in paragraph 19 when you just put, how can you describe it, you can find it in the other statement where I have said I had described him approximately how he looked to me then and I may repeat it to you and why he got the pseudonym, because of a movie that was being played in Albanian television. There was a character in that movie whose name was Qerqiz Topoli.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because as a Serbian police officer you should know better than to try and avoid answering question. The problem here is that you say in second statement that you were told to "follow him," not get in a car with him and a have a conversation. So your story has changed and I'm suggesting to you you were never in a car with him, at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour. That is -- the counsel is arguing with the witness. If the witness -- the witness can be given an opportunity to answer the question and explain. Secondly, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that had been done. And where Mr. Topolski had reached was with reason, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I accept your ruling, Your Honour. The second point is that on paragraph 20 there is actually an answer to the description issue that appears there. The witness does answer the question about the description and perhaps my learned colleague has simply neglected to look down to the bottom of paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could you answer my question now why it says that you followed him in a car whereas you said in your first statement that you were in a car with him and have told this Tribunal you were in a car with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski, it doesn't quite say that. It said he was told to follow him. You're assuming that occurred, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's getting late in the date I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It's getting late and if it's a bad point I'm not going to labour it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be a perfectly good point but let's get to it fairly and squarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour may have just spoiled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you in a car with Qerqiz, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And you do say that he had a beard at that time later on in paragraph 20. It was a very substantial beard he had, wasn't it, this man, Qerqiz, a big beard?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beard, the big beard you say, might be one -- one span of a hand, it might be half a metre, I don't know. It was a beard, a full beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You described in -- I'm' moving away from that to my last topic very briefly. You described in your evidence earlier on today regarding your arrest by the Serbs in, I think, December of 1998 and your subsequent imprisonment. It's right, isn't it, that you made a long statement to the Serbs in December of 1998?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't give them any long -- any statement, but I don't know myself what -- what statement is about. I never read any statement. I only signed something they told me to sign and where it was signed as they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, again, I don't want to waste yours or anyone else's time unnecessarily. Disclosed to us is a five- or six-page statement allegedly signed by you that contains a lot of information regarding names and details of terrorists as they're described, I think. Are you saying that this statement was written for you and you simply signed it?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said here that even today I don't what this statement comprised. I was forced to sign it after I was arrested. I know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't put it to you in those circumstances. I accept of course what you say about it. And finally I just want to ask you this: On Friday you gave evidence regarding a further meeting that took place in a room in Klecka, do you remember this, at which meeting people such as a you say Gazetari and Kumanova were present at which there was a discussion regarding units and reports and so on. Do you remember telling us at some length about this meeting on Friday?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You would have heard Mr. Shin, the gentleman who was asking you question on Friday and today answer a question from me at the end of Friday's proceedings when he indicated to the Court that it was the view of the Prosecution that Qerqiz was present at that meeting. I just want you to confirm, please, something that you have told us -- you've told us, not Mr. Shin -- today. It's your evidence, is it, that you are not at all sure whether Qerqiz was at that meeting or not. Is it that the position?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot tell you whether he was or not inside that room where we had the meeting with Celiku. He might have been, he might not. He might have enter that the room and he might have left that room. I didn't follow that, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That meeting itself would have had to have happened, wouldn't it, after the fall of Lapusnik on the 25th or 26th of July. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So perhaps we can leave things with you on a note of agreement, Witness, if we can. Would you agree with this: That you, as you sit here now, cannot be at all sure whether or not Qerqiz was there. Can we agree that is the position between us?

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "there"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In the meeting, participating in the meeting. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: Witness Shefqet Kabashi [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I explained it earlier. If you want, I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Oh no. I certainly don't want you to repeat yourself. Thank you. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No questions from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Shin I ventured that we would break at about ten to but there seems little point if trying to spend five or six minutes getting in a new witness and getting going. So we will resume tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- at 2.15 unless a need for special sitting to be squeezed in and delay us yet again. Sir, I'm pleased to be able to tell that you that is the completion of your evidence. You are now free to leave and return to your home. We thank you for your assistance in coming here and spending the time that you had to spend here. We will adjourn now and resume at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of March, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.45 p.m.,
